science: Tracing indirect feeding relationships in a food web.
meta: Noticing when you've only followed one link of a chain.
vignette: Instead of only asking what happens to rabbits if foxes disappear, add a second question: “How confident are you that you've traced every connection, not just the first one? What made you stop looking — ran out of ideas, or unsure how to check?” The second question isn't about ecosystems at all; it asks the student to inspect their own reasoning.

science: Ecosystems as networks, not chains.
meta: Naming systems thinking as a specific, learnable habit.
vignette: Tell the class directly: “Today isn't just about ecosystems — we're practising systems thinking, where you deliberately look for effects more than one step away. You'll use this again outside science.” Post two learning intentions side by side: the content one and the thinking one, so neither is left implicit.

science: Predicting flow-on effects of removing a species.
meta: Planning a reasoning strategy before diving in.
vignette: Before a ‘what if’ scenario, give students a two-column planner: Direct effects / Indirect effects (one step removed). Frame it as a general strategy for any rippling-change question, not an ecosystems worksheet. Ask: “What's your plan for not stopping at the first effect?”

science: Working through a food-web disturbance.
meta: Making the 'getting stuck and re-checking' moment visible.
vignette: Think aloud through an unfamiliar web: “Remove the small fish … algae grows … wait, that also changes what the larger fish eat — I need to go back and check that.” The pause at ‘wait’ is the point, not the final correct answer.

science: A food web with a non-obvious keystone species.
meta: Self-testing whether first-instinct reasoning holds up.
vignette: Once simple chains are secure, give a scenario where the obvious answer is wrong — a species that seems minor but supports several others. Students write their first-instinct answer, then revisit it: “Has anything changed your mind? What made you look again?”

science: Explaining energy flow and interdependence.
meta: Judging your own reasoning, not just the science answer.
vignette: Give a two-line self-rating: “I can identify producers, consumers and decomposers” (content) and “I checked for indirect effects before I finished” (thinking). Most students have never been asked to grade the second kind of statement.

science: Comparing food-web predictions in groups.
meta: Noticing other people's reasoning strategies differ from your own.
vignette: After individual predictions, ask groups: “Did anyone think about this differently to you? What did they check that you didn't?” The goal isn't consensus on the ecosystem question — it's seeing an unfamiliar strategy in action.

science: Repeated disturbance scenarios across a unit.
meta: Building a reusable habit of checking for indirect effects.
vignette: Reuse the direct/indirect planner across unrelated food webs — grassland, then rainforest, then marine — so the thinking habit gets rehearsed, not just memory of one system.

science: Progress through the Living Systems focus area.
meta: Checking whether the habit is becoming automatic.
vignette: Ask periodically: “When you saw a new food web today, did you automatically check for indirect effects, or did you have to remind yourself?” The shift from reminded to automatic is your evidence, more than any single quiz mark.

science: Identifying independent, dependent and controlled variables.
meta: Interrogating your own draft plan before anyone else does.
vignette: Before a method is submitted, require three self-directed questions: “What exactly am I changing? What exactly am I measuring? What am I deliberately keeping the same?” Some students can define ‘variable’ correctly yet never turn that definition into a question about their own plan.

science: The structure of a fair test.
meta: Naming planning discipline as a transferable habit, not a one-off worksheet.
vignette: Say directly: “This variable-identification skill is what you'll use in every practical this year, and in your depth study. The topic changes; the habit of asking these three questions first doesn't.”

science: Drafting a method for a chosen investigation.
meta: Using a reusable scaffold instead of starting from a blank page.
vignette: Provide one content-free planning template — question / variables / equipment / steps / safety / expected pattern — reused for every investigation all year. The template's familiarity, not its content, is what carries the metacognitive value.

science: Spotting an uncontrolled variable in a draft method.
meta: Verbalising the checking process, not just presenting the fix.
vignette: Draft a flawed method on the board and think aloud: “I said I'm testing temperature’s effect on rate … but I haven't fixed the concentration each time. If I don't control that, I won't know which variable caused the change. Let me add that.” Students see the catch, not only the corrected version.

science: Designing for a genuinely open question, no single obvious variable.
meta: Testing whether the planning routine survives without heavy scaffolding.
vignette: Once students use the template confidently on a familiar topic, hand them an unfamiliar everyday question with no template, and ask them to reconstruct the three planning questions from memory.

science: A completed investigation method.
meta: Grading your own planning process, separately from your results.
vignette: Before conducting the investigation, students self-check: “Did I identify all three variable types? Did I check for a fair test?” Doing this before results arrive keeps the self-assessment about the plan, not about whether the experiment ‘worked’.

science: Peer review of a draft method.
meta: Recognising other students catch different planning gaps than you do.
vignette: Swap draft plans in pairs; each partner finds one thing the writer missed using the three-question routine. Not for marking — for noticing which question each of them defaults to, and which they forget.

science: Repeated investigations across topics and stages.
meta: Reducing reliance on the template over time.
vignette: Informally track how much of the template a class still needs written in front of them versus generated unprompted by mid-year. The goal is visible scaffolding withdrawal, not a new skill each time.

science: Investigation design across a term.
meta: Checking whether the routine has become a default habit.
vignette: Before planning starts, ask: “Without me saying anything — what are your first three questions?” If the class can recite the routine unprompted, that's evidence it's a genuine habit, not a compliance step.

science: Judging a study's quality — sample size, method, conflicts of interest.
meta: Asking why a claim feels convincing, before asking if it's true.
vignette: Before evaluating whether a claim is right, ask: “What about this source made you want to believe it — and is that a good reason?” This separates a persuasive source from a reliable one, and turns the inspection back onto the student's own reaction.

science: Criteria for reliable evidence — sample size, replication, source.
meta: Naming source evaluation as a specific, nameable habit of mind.
vignette: State directly: “We're building one particular skill today — noticing when a claim outruns its evidence. This isn't about memorising these examples; it's a habit for every science headline you'll ever read.”

science: Comparing two conflicting sources on the same claim.
meta: Deciding what to check before reading, not while being persuaded.
vignette: Before reading either source, students write three questions they'll ask of each — who funded it, sample size, has it been repeated — fixing the criteria before the content of either source can sway them.

science: A credible-sounding source with a methodological flaw.
meta: Narrating the moment of nearly being persuaded too quickly.
vignette: Read a claim aloud and think aloud: “That sounds convincing … wait, it says ‘a study found’ but not how many people. I nearly accepted that without checking. Let me look for that detail first.” The catch is the modelled behaviour, not the final verdict.

science: A well-evidenced claim that conflicts with a common student belief.
meta: Noticing when you're grading evidence differently because you dislike the conclusion.
vignette: Deliberately include one well-supported claim that cuts against a common assumption, then ask: “Are you using the same standard of evidence as last time — or is this one harder to accept because you didn't expect it?”

science: A completed evidence-evaluation task.
meta: Checking your conclusion against your own criteria, not your gut.
vignette: Students revisit their own planned questions and tick off whether they actually used each one, or fell back to gut feeling under time pressure.

science: Comparing verdicts on the same source in groups.
meta: Seeing that people can weigh identical evidence differently.
vignette: Groups compare verdicts on the same source, not to reach one correct answer, but to ask: “What did someone else in your group notice that you missed?”

science: Repeated tasks across health, environment and technology claims.
meta: Building a durable habit that isn't topic-specific.
vignette: Vary the subject matter deliberately across the term so students rehearse the underlying evaluative habit, rather than becoming expert judges of one particular topic.

science: Evidence evaluation across a unit.
meta: Checking whether the habit triggers outside the classroom.
vignette: Ask periodically: “Has anyone caught themselves asking these questions about an ad or a social media claim outside class?” Self-reported transfer is a strong sign the habit, not just the content, has stuck.

science: Distinguishing 'stopped' from 'still moving both ways at equal rates'.
meta: Noticing which mental picture you're actually using.
vignette: After a correct-sounding answer, ask: “When you pictured that just then, was anything still moving, or had it gone still?” Many students give textbook wording while still picturing a static system — the question targets the picture, not the vocabulary.

science: Dynamic equilibrium and Le Chatelier's principle.
meta: Naming the exact misconception being replaced.
vignette: State the misconception before the correct model: “Almost everyone starts out picturing equilibrium as ‘stopped’. That's specifically what we're replacing today, not adding on top of.” Naming it gives students something concrete to check their own thinking against.

science: Predicting a Le Chatelier shift for an unfamiliar stress.
meta: Using a deliberate step-by-step check instead of pattern-matching.
vignette: Fix a sequence before answering: “1) What's the stress? 2) Which direction relieves it? 3) Does that match my first guess?” Planning the steps first catches a wrong instinct instead of locking it in.

science: A Kc calculation next to a conceptual shift question.
meta: Showing that each calls for a different kind of checking.
vignette: Switch between the two aloud: “For the calculation I'm checking units and my ICE table. For the shift question I'm checking my mental model, not a formula — a completely different mistake to look for.” Naming the difference stops quantitative habits leaking into conceptual reasoning.

science: A scenario with two simultaneous stresses.
meta: Self-testing whether understanding holds when more than one variable moves.
vignette: Once single-variable shifts are secure, present two simultaneous stresses and ask students to predict, then name which part of their reasoning they were least sure of — uncertainty as diagnostic information, not something to hide.

science: Understanding of dynamic equilibrium after a block of lessons.
meta: Telling apart 'I can define it' from 'I've stopped picturing it as static'.
vignette: Self-rate against two separate lines: “I can define dynamic equilibrium” and “If I'm honest, I still sometimes picture the reaction as stopped.” The second line targets the actual misconception, not recall of the definition.

science: Comparing predicted shifts in pairs.
meta: Explaining your reasoning aloud as a check on your own understanding.
vignette: Students explain a prediction to a partner using only “the system responds by …” — if they can't finish the sentence without falling back to “it just goes that way”, both partners now know the reasoning isn't secure yet.

science: Repeated shift predictions across different reaction systems.
meta: Rehearsing the step-by-step check until it's automatic.
vignette: Reuse the three-step check — stress / direction / match my instinct — across several unrelated reactions over consecutive lessons, so it stops needing re-teaching every time a new reaction appears.

science: Understanding of equilibrium in the lead-up to assessment.
meta: Checking whether the misconception has gone, not just gone quiet.
vignette: A few lessons out from assessment, ask directly: “If you had to bet — is any part of you still tempted by ‘equilibrium means stopped’?” Misconceptions often go underground rather than disappearing; a direct check surfaces them while there's time to act.
